config.title: Generic useFetch<T>

intro.title: Generic useFetch<T>
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a reusable custom React hook called `useFetch<T>` that fetches data from an API. You will learn how to use TypeScript generics to make the hook flexible and type-safe, allowing it to return data of any specified type. The lesson involves key React concepts like state management with `useState` and side effects with `useEffect`. By the end, you'll have a powerful hook that handles loading states, errors, and typed data fetching for use in any component.
intro.usecase: The generic useFetch<T> hook is essential in modern React applications that consume diverse APIs, such as e-commerce platforms displaying products, user profiles, and order histories with different data structures. In admin dashboards, developers use it to fetch analytics data, user lists, and system metrics while maintaining type safety across multiple endpoints. This pattern appears in social media feeds loading posts, comments, and notifications, where each data type requires specific TypeScript interfaces. By implementing useFetch<T>, developers write reusable data-fetching logic once and apply it throughout their application, reducing code duplication and ensuring consistent error handling and loading states.

objectives: Implement a generic TypeScript interface for API response data
Construct a generic React hook with type parameters for fetching data
Initialize state variables with proper generic typing for loading, error, and data
Apply type-safe error handling within the generic fetch hook
Render components using the generic hook with specific data types
Configure the hook to accept custom URL parameters while maintaining type safety
Manipulate and transform fetched data using generic type constraints

steps.title: Import React and all hooks needed for this lesson (useState, useEffect)
steps.instruction: Import React, useState, and useEffect from 'react'.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the two hooks we'll need for our custom fetch hook.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

steps.title: Define the FetchState<T> interface for type safety
steps.instruction: Below the imports, define a generic TypeScript interface named FetchState<T> with three properties: data (type T | null), loading (type boolean), and error (type string | null).
steps.hint: Remember to use the generic type parameter <T> after the interface name. The data property should accept either type T or null.
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

// Define the FetchState<T> interface here
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a generic interface that describes the shape of the fetch state, enabling type safety for data, loading, and error states.
successCriteria: The FetchState<T> interface is defined with the correct generic type parameter and three properties: data (T | null), loading (boolean), error (string | null).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Check that your interface includes all three required properties with the correct types: data (T | null), loading (boolean), and error (string | null).
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface definition is missing or incorrect. Ensure you define a generic interface named FetchState<T> with the three specified properties.

steps.title: Create the useFetch<T> custom hook function signature
steps.instruction: Create a function named useFetch that is a generic custom hook. It should take a url parameter of type string and return a FetchState<T>. Use the arrow function syntax or function declaration.
steps.hint: Start by writing the function signature with the generic type parameter <T> before the parameter list. The return type should be FetchState<T>.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named useFetch with proper TypeScript generic syntax that matches the signature: useFetch<T>(url: string): FetchState<T>
successCriteria: The useFetch function is declared with generic type <T>, accepts a url parameter of type string, and specifies a return type of FetchState<T>
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your function has the generic type parameter <T>, takes a url parameter of type string, and specifies the return type as FetchState<T>.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature doesn't match the expected pattern. Remember to create a function named useFetch with generic type <T> that takes a url string parameter and returns FetchState<T>.

steps.title: Initialize state with useState inside useFetch<T>
steps.instruction: Inside the useFetch function, call useState with the generic type FetchState<T> to initialize state. Set the initial state to an object with data: null, loading: true, and error: null.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with the generic type you defined earlier. The initial state should match the FetchState<T> interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook now has a state variable initialized with proper typing and default values.
successCriteria: useState is called with generic type FetchState<T> and initial state { data: null, loading: true, error: null }.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're using the FetchState<T> generic type and setting all three properties in the initial state.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check that you're calling useState with the correct generic type and initial state object.

steps.instruction: Inside the useFetch<T> hook, define an async function named fetchData that will handle the fetch operation.
steps.hint: Create an async function that will later be called to fetch data. For now, just define it with an empty body.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook should contain an async function declaration named fetchData.
successCriteria: An async function named fetchData is defined inside the useFetch hook.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you've defined an async function named fetchData inside the useFetch hook.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData async function is not defined correctly. Check that it's inside the useFetch hook and uses the async keyword.

steps.title: Call fetchData inside useEffect
steps.instruction: Add a useEffect hook inside your useFetch function that calls the fetchData function when the url changes.
steps.hint: Use useEffect with the url as a dependency to trigger the fetchData function whenever the URL changes.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useEffect hook should be added to call fetchData when the URL changes.
successCriteria: useEffect is implemented with fetchData called inside and url in the dependency array.

steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure useEffect calls fetchData and includes url in the dependency array.

steps.title: Return the state from useFetch<T>
steps.instruction: Return the state object from the useFetch hook to make the fetch data available to components that use this hook.
steps.hint: The state object contains data, loading, and error properties. Simply return it at the end of the hook.
steps.expectedOutcome: The useFetch hook now returns the state object, making the fetch data accessible to consuming components.
successCriteria: The useFetch hook returns the state object containing data, loading, and error properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.hint: Use the state object returned by useFetch<User> to check loading, error, and data properties. Render appropriate JSX for each case.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will display 'Loading...' while fetching, show an error message if the fetch fails, or display the user's name and email when data is available.
